title: The Water of Life
paragraphs: Long before you or I were born, in a land far, far away, there lived a king who had three sons. Once this king fell sick—so sick that nobody thought he would survive. His sons were deeply grieved by their father’s illness, and as they walked together in the palace garden, sunk in gloom, a little old man came up to them and asked what was wrong. They told him their father was gravely ill and they feared nothing could save him. “I know what could,” said the little old man. “The Water of Life. One drink of it and he would be well again. But it is very hard to get.” The eldest son said, “I’ll soon find it,” and he went to the sick king and begged to be allowed to go in search of the Water of Life, since it was the only thing that could save him. “No,” said the king. “I would rather die than send you into the great danger you would face on such a journey.” But the son pleaded so hard that the king gave in, and the prince thought to himself, “If I bring my father this water, he will make me the sole heir to his kingdom.”

So he set out, and after he had traveled for some time he came to a deep valley hemmed in by rocks and woods. Looking around, he saw a little ugly dwarf standing on a rock above him, wearing a sugarloaf cap and a scarlet cloak. The dwarf called down to him, “Prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” “What business is that of yours, you ugly imp?” the prince said haughtily, and rode on.

The dwarf was furious at this rudeness and cast a fairy spell of bad luck on him. As the prince rode on, the mountain pass grew narrower and narrower, until at last it was so tight that he couldn’t take another step forward. When he tried to turn his horse around and go back the way he had come, a loud laugh rang out all around him, and he found the path closed off behind him, so that he was shut in on every side. Next he tried to get off his horse and make his way on foot, but again the laugh rang in his ears, and he found he couldn’t move a single step. So he had no choice but to stay there, held by the spell.

Meanwhile the old king lingered on, hoping every day for his son’s return, until at last the second son said, “Father, I’ll go and look for the Water of Life.” For he thought, “My brother must be dead, and the kingdom will come to me if I find the water.” The king was very reluctant at first to let him go, but in the end he gave way. So the second son set out along the same road his brother had taken, and he met the same elf, who stopped him at the same place in the mountains and said, as before, “Prince, prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” “Mind your own business, you busybody!” said the prince scornfully, and rode on.

But the dwarf put the same spell on him that he had put on his older brother, and he, too, ended up trapped in the heart of the mountains. That is how it goes with proud, foolish people who think they are above everyone else and are too proud to ask for advice or accept it.

After the second prince had been gone a long time, the youngest son said he would go and search for the Water of Life, and he was sure he would soon be able to make his father well again. So he set out, and the dwarf met him too, at the same spot in the valley among the mountains, and said, “Prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” The prince answered, “I’m looking for the Water of Life, because my father is ill and close to death. Can you help me? Please be kind and help me if you can!” “Do you know where to find it?” asked the dwarf. “No,” said the prince, “I don’t. Please tell me, if you know.” “Then, since you have spoken to me kindly and have the sense to ask for advice, I will tell you how and where to go. The water you want flows from a well in an enchanted castle. So that you can reach it safely, I will give you an iron wand and two small loaves of bread. Strike the iron door of the castle three times with the wand, and it will open. Inside, two hungry lions will be lying with their jaws open, waiting for prey, but if you throw them the bread, they will let you pass. Then hurry to the well and take some of the Water of Life before the clock strikes twelve, because if you stay any longer, the door will shut on you forever.”

The prince thanked his little friend in the scarlet cloak for his help. He took the wand and the bread and traveled on and on, over sea and over land, until he reached the end of his journey and found everything just as the dwarf had said. The door flew open at the third stroke of the wand, and once the lions were calmed he went on through the castle and came at last to a beautiful hall. In it he saw several knights sitting in a trance, and he pulled off their rings and put them on his own fingers. In another room he saw a sword and a loaf of bread lying on a table, and he took those too. Farther on he came to a room where a beautiful young lady sat on a couch. She welcomed him joyfully and said that if he freed her from the spell that bound her, the kingdom would be his, provided he came back in a year and married her. Then she told him that the well holding the Water of Life was in the palace gardens, and she urged him to hurry and draw what he needed before the clock struck twelve.

He walked on, and as he passed through beautiful gardens he came to a lovely, shady spot with a couch in it. Feeling tired, he thought he would rest a while and gaze at the lovely scenery around him. So he lay down, and sleep overtook him without his noticing, and he didn’t wake until the clock was striking a quarter to twelve. He jumped up from the couch, horribly frightened, ran to the well, filled a cup that stood beside him with water, and rushed to get out in time. Just as he was passing through the iron door, the clock struck twelve, and the door slammed shut so fast that it snapped off a piece of his heel.

Once he was safe, he was overjoyed to have the Water of Life, and as he headed homeward he passed the little dwarf again. When the dwarf saw the sword and the loaf, he said, “You have won a fine prize. With the sword you can cut down whole armies in a single blow, and the bread will never run out.” Then the prince thought, “I can’t go home to my father without my brothers.” So he said, “My dear friend, can you tell me where my two brothers are? They set out to find the Water of Life before I did, and they never came back.” “I have trapped them by a charm between two mountains,” said the dwarf, “because they were proud and badly behaved, and they scorned to ask for advice.” The prince pleaded so hard for his brothers that the dwarf finally freed them, though unwillingly, saying, “Beware of them, for they have wicked hearts.” Their brother, however, was very glad to see them, and he told them everything that had happened to him: how he had found the Water of Life and taken a cupful of it, how he had freed a beautiful princess from the spell that bound her, and how she had promised to wait a whole year and then marry him and give him the kingdom.

Then the three of them rode on together, and on the way home they came to a country devastated by war and a terrible famine, so that everyone feared they would all die of want. The prince gave the king of that land the bread, and his whole kingdom ate from it. He also lent the king the wonderful sword, and the king used it to destroy the enemy’s army, and so the kingdom was at peace again and had plenty to eat. In the same way he helped two other countries they passed through on the road.

When they reached the sea, they boarded a ship. During the voyage the two older brothers said to each other, “Our brother has found the water that we couldn’t find. So our father will cast us off and give him the kingdom, which is rightfully ours.” They were consumed with envy and a hunger for revenge, and they agreed together on how to ruin him. They waited until he was fast asleep, then poured the Water of Life out of his cup and kept it for themselves, filling his cup with bitter seawater instead.

When they reached home, the youngest son brought his cup to the sick king so that he could drink and be healed. But he had barely tasted the bitter seawater when he grew even worse than before. Then the two older sons came in and accused the youngest of what they themselves had done. They claimed that he meant to poison their father, and that they were the ones who had found the Water of Life and brought it back. The moment the king began to drink what they gave him, he felt his sickness leave him, and he was as strong and well as in his youth. Then the two went to their brother and laughed at him. “So, brother, you found the Water of Life, did you?” they said. “You did the work, and we get the reward. With all your cleverness, why couldn’t you keep your eyes open? Next year one of us will take your beautiful princess away, if you don’t watch out. You’d better not say a word of this to our father, because he doesn’t believe anything you say. And if you tell tales, you’ll lose your life as well. Keep quiet, and we’ll let you off.”

The old king was still furious with his youngest son. He believed the boy had truly meant to take his life, so he summoned his court and asked what should be done, and everyone agreed that the prince must die. The prince knew nothing of this until one day, when the king’s chief huntsman took him hunting. Alone with him in the forest, the prince noticed how sad the huntsman looked and asked, “My friend, what is wrong?” “I can’t tell you, and I don’t dare,” said the huntsman. But the prince pleaded with him. “Just tell me what it is,” he said, “and don’t worry that I’ll be angry. I will forgive you.” “Alas,” said the huntsman, “the king has ordered me to shoot you.” The prince flinched at this, then said, “Spare my life, and I’ll trade clothes with you. You can take my royal coat back to my father as proof, and give me your shabby one.” “Gladly,” said the huntsman. “I’m happy to save you, since I could never have shot you anyway.” So he took the prince’s coat, handed over his own shabby one, and walked away through the forest.

Some time later, three grand embassies arrived at the old king’s court, bringing rich gifts of gold and precious stones for his youngest son. They had been sent by the three kings to whom the prince had lent his sword and his loaf of bread, to rid them of their enemy and feed their people. This touched the old king’s heart. He began to think his son might be innocent after all, and he said to his court, “If only my son were still alive! How it grieves me that I had him killed!” “He is alive,” said the huntsman. “I’m glad I took pity on him. I let him go in peace and brought home his royal coat.” The king was overwhelmed with joy, and he announced throughout his whole kingdom that if his son would come back to court, he would forgive him.

In the meantime the princess was eagerly waiting for her deliverer to return. She had a road built leading up to her palace, made entirely of shining gold, and she told her courtiers that whoever came riding straight up that road to the gate was her true love, and they were to let him in. But anyone who rode beside the road, they could be sure, was not the right man, and they were to send him away at once.

Before long the eldest brother decided to hurry to the princess and claim that he was the one who had freed her, and that he should therefore have her as his wife, and the kingdom along with her. When he reached the palace and saw the golden road, he stopped to admire it. “It would be a shame to ride on such a beautiful road,” he thought, and he turned aside and rode along its right-hand edge. But when he got to the gate, the guards, who had watched which way he came, told him he could not be who he claimed to be, and that he should go on his way.

Soon afterward the second prince set off on the same errand. When he reached the golden road and his horse had put one hoof on it, he stopped to look, found it very beautiful, and said to himself, “What a shame it would be for anything to trample this!” So he too turned aside and rode along the left edge. But when he reached the gate, the guards said he was not the true prince, and that he too must go away. And away he went.

When a full year had gone by, the third brother came out of the forest where he had been hiding from his father’s anger, and set out to find his promised bride. He traveled along thinking of her the whole way, and rode so fast that he never even noticed what the road was made of. He simply rode his horse straight over it, and as he reached the gate it swung open. The princess welcomed him joyfully and declared that he was her deliverer, and would now be her husband and lord of the kingdom. When their first happiness at meeting had passed, the princess told him she had heard that his father had forgiven him and wanted him home. So before the wedding he went to see his father, and took her with him. He told the king everything: how his brothers had cheated and robbed him, and how he had put up with all those wrongs out of love for his father. The old king was furious and wanted to punish his wicked sons, but they got away. They boarded a ship and sailed off across the wide sea, and where they went, nobody knew and nobody cared.

Then the old king called his court together and invited his whole kingdom to the wedding of his son and the princess. Young and old, nobles and squires, gentle folk and common, all came at once when the summons went out. Among them came the friendly dwarf, in his sugarloaf hat and a new scarlet cloak.

The wedding was held, and the merry bells rang.
And all the good people, they danced and they sang,
And feasted and frolicked, I can’t say how long.
